conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that taking vitamin C regularly does not meaningfully prevent colds in the general population, citing systematic review evidence that shows no effect on cold incidence.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** Your answer is broadly correct for the general population: taking vitamin C regularly does **not meaningfully prevent people from getting colds**.

The strongest evidence supplied is a Cochrane systematic review of placebo-controlled trials (at least 200 mg/day). Across 29 comparisons involving 11,306 participants, regular vitamin C had **no effect on cold incidence in the ordinary population**. An earlier pooled estimate was risk ratio **0.96 (95% CI 0.92–1.00)**—at most a small, borderline reduction that does not support routine prevention use.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub2/abstract

That does not mean vitamin C has no effect at all. Regular supplementation modestly shortened cold duration—about **8% in adults** and **14% in children**—and reduced severity. This is a treatment-burden benefit among people who do get colds, rather than convincing prevention of infections.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4/full

There is an important exception: Cochrane’s conclusion notes potential usefulness for people exposed to **brief periods of severe physical exercise**—a population unlike most community-dwelling adults.  

So, for most people, routine vitamin C—especially “mega-dose” use—should not be expected to stop colds. It may slightly reduce how long or how severe a cold is if taken regularly, but that is a different claim from prevention.
